source: Discharging and Energy in RC Circuits
A capacitor discharges as q = Q₀e^(−t/RC), and all of its stored energy ends up as heat in the resistor.
Students think the time to lose half the charge depends on how much charge there was at the start.

Disconnect the battery from a charged capacitor and connect the capacitor across a resistor instead. Charge flows from one plate, through the resistor, to the other, and the capacitor empties. The equation is even simpler than charging, and its solution has a striking property: a fixed "half-life".

Around the loop the capacitor's voltage drives the current through the resistor: $\dfrac{q}{C} = IR$. The current drains the charge, $I = -\dfrac{dq}{dt}$, so
        $$\frac{dq}{dt} = -\frac{q}{RC}.$$
        The charge drains at a rate proportional to how much is left. Whenever "rate is proportional to amount", the solution is an exponential, $q = Q_0e^{-t/RC}$, the same law as radioactive decay.

$$q = Q_0e^{-t/RC}, \qquad V = V_0e^{-t/RC}, \qquad I = \frac{V_0}{R}e^{-t/RC}.$$
        The charge halves every $t_{1/2} = RC\ln 2 \approx 0.693\,RC$, however much there is. All of the stored energy, $\tfrac{1}{2}CV_0^2$, ends up as heat in the resistor.
Discharging from two different starting voltages: both curves reach half their start at the same moment, $t_{1/2} = RC\ln 2$. The dotted curve is the stored energy, which halves twice as fast.
Worked examples
A $100\ \mu\text{F}$ capacitor charged to $50\ \text{V}$ discharges through $10\ \text{k}\Omega$. How much charge is left after $2.0\ \text{s}$, and what is the current then?
Charge left after a while
$q \approx 677\ \text{μC}$
How long does it take the charge to halve, and then to fall to a quarter?
The half time
$t_{1/2} \approx 0.693\ \text{s}$
A quarter is half of half: another $0.693\ \text{s}$, so $1.39\ \text{s}$ in all.
How much energy does the resistor turn into heat over the whole discharge?
All the energy becomes heat
$$\int_0^\infty I^2R\,dt = \frac{V_0^2}{R}\int_0^\infty e^{-2t/RC}\,dt = \frac{V_0^2}{R}\cdot\frac{RC}{2} = \tfrac{1}{2}CV_0^2$$
$\tfrac{1}{2}(100 \times 10^{-6})(50)^2 = 0.125\ \text{J}$: exactly the energy the capacitor started with.

This gives a neat way to measure $RC$ in a lab. Take the natural log of the voltage: $\ln V = \ln V_0 - t/RC$. Plotted against time, $\ln V$ falls along a straight line with slope $-1/RC$. Two readings are enough in principle: $RC = \dfrac{t_2 - t_1}{\ln(V_1/V_2)}$, and the starting voltage cancels out.

"A capacitor with more charge takes longer to lose half of it." More charge means a higher voltage, which drives a bigger current, so it drains faster in exact proportion. The half time is $RC\ln 2$, with no $Q_0$ in it. Check with the visual: two capacitors starting at different voltages reach half their starting values together.
